page.description:
I have conducted an audit of Anthropic's finances.

What I have found is so shocking that I am calling for a Congressional investigation.

Anthropic is not just seeking regulatory capture.

It has built a regulatory capture machine that cannot be turned off.

Structural financial incentives make it impossible for Anthropic -- I call it the Anthropic Network -- to turn off its own AI doom cycle.

It starts with METR.

Dario Amodei proposes "third-party evaluators" to assess the risk of Anthropic's models.

He proposes METR for this purpose.

But METR is financially dependent on the Anthropic's success -- specifically, on the explosive growth of more than $7 billion dollars in Anthropic stock.

Dustin Moskovitz invested this stock into Good Ventures Foundation, where it represents the majority of that organization's portfolio.

And GVF is the overwhelming funder of the entire Anthropic Network ecosystem.

This stock was worth $500 million early last year.

It is worth more than $7.7 billion just ~16 months later.

METR -- and all of those building a career its parent organizations -- cannot afford to disrupt that growth.

Because if Anthropic goes under, many of the organizations that fund METR go under as well.

But if Anthropic succeeds, METR and its parent organizations become more richly financed to regulate AI -- something those at METR want very much.

The "third-party evaluator" is not "third-party" at all.

The evaluator is on Anthropic's payroll.

If this were the end of it, that's bad.

But that isn't all.

The same organizations that fund METR also fund the many organizations, such as the Tarbell Center, that promote AI Doom.

The Tarbell Center publishes AI Doom articles in The Verge, Science, LA Times, The Dispatch, TIME, and others.

They are selling the problem, and then selling the solution to the problem -- from the same money pile: Anthropic's.

All of these organizations are financially dependent on the same exploding $7 billion money pile.

As Anthropic grows more and more powerful, its AI Doom Machine grows better and better financed -- louder and louder.

Meanwhile, the regulatory regime seeded in METR grows larger to solve the increasingly loud -- now hysterical -- problem of AI Doom that the Anthropic Network itself created.

From this standpoint, as Anthropic becomes more powerful, AI might be getting scarier, sure -- but the positive feedback loop also becomes more deafening -- independent of objective facts.

This itself is an objective fact.

The deafening AI Doom is part of an business model, that, as it expands, so too does the AI Doom messaging -- there is simply more money to do it.

But the problem also goes in the other direction:

If Anthropic dies, the Regulatory Regime and the AI Doom Machine are crippled or die.

Neither METR nor Tarbell nor the other organizations in the Anthropic Network can allow that to happen.

Hence, neither METR or the AI Doom Machine can be trusted to provide independent assessments of Anthropic's models or AI more broadly.

They simply are not organizations independent of Anthropic.

And Anthropic cannot detach itself from METR or Tarbell or countless other safety orgs (not shown here), either, because they drive hype for the models and the possibility of eventual regulatory capture, and Anthropic will not give that up willingly.

What's more, the people at all of these organizations are all the same ecosystem, the same community. They just shuffle between organizations.

The Anthropic Network is therefore, so long as it is successful, locked into a self-amplifying feedback loop inside an ideological monoculture.

And that feedback loop is winning.

That's what Jacob Coxon is.

China is keeping messaging tight. That is why optimism for AI is so high in China.

America has Anthropic: a massive company pushing anti-AI propaganda at a state level.

Anthropic will either create hysteria until American AI slows down and China wins, or it will create fractures throughout American society with severe political consequences.

Ironically, because of the structural financial incentives underpinning the Anthropic Network, it has become the same kind of self-amplifying virus that it fantasizes AI to become in the future -- while hiding its tracks just as carefully.

It is the mirror of the same AI virus that it hypothesizes to consume America.

Anthropic's business model, models itself after the very thing it claims to fear.

Except Anthropic's ideology infects humans, not computers.

Congress must investigate.

Evidence and Github in next post.

Then some supplementary figures.

There is no single mathematical definition, rather there are a number of curves that fit this shape. All general squircles are parametrized, and can vary between circle and square. A good choice is the coordinates of the midpoint of the quadrant, assuming a unit radius; here 𝑥 and 𝑦 are equal. The conversion formula is simple and intuitive: 𝑥 = 0.5 1 / 𝑛 . page.text_excerpt: Anton Zhiyanov projectsbooksblogabout◐ Probabilistic data structures in Go Probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle. Does the set contain a certain item? How many unique items are in the collection? Which items appear most often? Unlike deterministic structures like sets and frequency tables, the answers might not be exact, but in return, you can drastically reduce memory usage. In this post, we'll talk about what probabilistic structures are, how they work, and what kinds of guarantees they provide. I'll also introduce unsure — a package that implements these structures in Go. It's simple (the core logic for each data structure is 100–300 LOC), fast (usually several times faster than other implementations), and has no dependencies except for the standard library. Bloom filter • Count-min sketch • HyperLogLog • T-digest • Top-k Bloom filter A Bloom filter is a set that trades certainty for space. It can tell you that an item is definitely not in the set, or that it probably is (which might be a false positive). The filter doesn't actually store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set. For example, a regular set with 1,000,000 distinct 8-byte strings takes about 64 MB. A Bloom filter for the same strings, with a 1% false positive rate, uses only 1.24 MB (about 10 bits per item) — that's 50 times smaller. The size of the filter doesn't depend on the item size, so the difference gets even bigger with longer strings. A Bloom filter often resides in memory and helps minimize expensive I/O operations such as disk reads or network calls. You check if an item is in the filter, and if the answer is "no", you skip the costly lookup. If the answer is "yes", you still have to perform the lookup because it might be a false positive. // A filter for 1000 items with a 1% false positive rate. filter := bloom.New(1000, 0.01) filter.Add([]byte("alice")) filter.Add([]byte("bob")) filter.Contains([]byte("alice"))

United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered what is reportedly its first mission failure in its 20-year history, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Leo is Amazon’s competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink, but it has struggled to get off the ground so far, putting only a small portion of the necessary satellites to challenge Starlink into orbit. Today’s launch was supposed to be the first of 38 flights Amazon purchased from ULA. Computer-aided design (CAD) software allows creators to design buildings, bridges, video game art, film monsters, 3D printable objects, and many other things before building a physical version of the design. At their core, CAD tools are a method of abstracting the 3-dimensional design into something that can be viewed and edited on a 2-dimensional screen. SUBSCRIBE October 19, 2026 Pangram is not an oracle by Emily In light of Vauhini Vara's accusation that Simbarashe Kundizeza's Caine prize-winning story “The Blue Fighter” was generated with an LLM (see Kundizeza’s response here), I want to write a bit about how evaluation works in the field of natural language processing (NLP) and what claims of “accuracy” of systems mean for interpreting the output of a given tool on a particular input. Today's case in point is Pangram, a tool which has found many willing users in the publishing industry, but this applies to synthetic text detection tools more generally. I keep hearing Pangram described as extremely “accurate”. This tells me that a) the company’s advertising is effective and b) we need some public education on what “accuracy” means with respect to language technology and how such technologies are evaluated. This post is going to be primarily about evaluation practice, but the larger story isn’t—the larger story is about racism, about the use of software sold as “AI” to clothe racism in a veneer of objectivity, and the continuing demands placed on racialized authors, especially Black authors, to establish credibility to impossible standards. Others, such as Adio Dinika and Samantha Asumadu are better positioned to write about that broader story than I am, and I encourage you to read their words. I want to acknowledge that the synthetic media, including text, flooding our information ecosystem is a real problem. I have been writing about this for a while and we also write about it in The AI Con. Editors and publishers who worked with her look back Melissa Denes Sun 15 Nov 2026 07.00 EST Share 113 Prefer the Guardian on Google P ublisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes. “But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.
